[Week 2 →](week-02.qmd)

**Slides (PDF):** [week01-introduction.pdf](slides/week01-introduction.pdf)

**If you are new to the topic**, start with:

- [What is LAE?](primer.qmd) — plain-English orientation  
- [How does LAE work?](business-overview.qmd) — roles in the value chain  
- [Who decides what?](regulators.qmd) — institutions and standing caveats  

**This week** defines LAE, introduces three tools — [**VOT**](glossary.qmd#value-of-time) (value of time), **generalized cost**, and [**NPV**](glossary.qmd#npv) (net present value) — maps who gets paid, and explains sandboxes. **Week 2** turns to market structure and competition.

## Summary {#summary}

**Before you go**

- What “low-altitude economy” means in plain English, and how it differs from traditional aviation.
- Jargon you will hear: LAE, UAM, and AAM (defined in §3).
- Simple tools for value of time, generalized cost, and whether a service might be commercially viable.
- Who sits in the ecosystem (who creates value, who gets paid) and why a regulatory sandbox matters for testing.

**Takeaways**

- LAE is a whole system: aircraft, infrastructure, digital systems, operators, customers, and supporting services.
- A service creates value when it saves time, cuts cost or risk, improves access, or enables a mission that other modes cannot do well.
- Viability hangs on willingness to pay, demand, utilization, load factor, operating cost, and investment cost.
- A sandbox supports controlled testing and faster learning. It does **not** remove safety or compliance needs.
- Technology matters when it improves the economics of the full service — not only the aircraft.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Classroom numbers vs absolute facts.** Worked examples below use round figures (fares, waiting times, cost shares). They are **illustrative assumptions for learning**, not current Hong Kong market data or forecasts. Absolute figures — Cap. 448G bands, OHKF **HK$350bn**, first-batch Sandbox **38 of 72**, Sandbox X module counts, UTM “from 2028” language — stay with their issuers on [Key figures](key-figures.qmd) / [Readings](#readings) / [Official status](tracker.qmd).
:::

## Learning objectives

By the end of Week 1 you should be able to:

1. **Define** the low-altitude economy (LAE) in plain English as a whole service system, not only as aircraft.  
2. **Distinguish** LAE from traditional airline aviation, and keep **LAE**, **UAM**, and **AAM** from collapsing into one label.  
3. **Identify** the main application families where LAE might create customer value.  
4. **Map** who creates value and who gets paid along a simple value chain.  
5. **Explain** what a Hong Kong regulatory sandbox is for — and what it does *not* waive — keeping the first **Regulatory Sandbox** separate from **Sandbox X**.  
6. **Use** simple tools — value of time, generalized cost, NPV intuition, and a unit-cost equation — to judge whether a service *might* be commercially viable.

### How this week is organised

| Part | Sections | Focus |
|------|----------|--------|
| Concepts | §§1–5 | What LAE is; jargon; value families; Hong Kong scale / HK$350bn attribution |
| Tools | §§6–8 | VOT, NPV, generalized cost; classroom worked examples; how tools connect |
| Industry & rules | §§9–12 | Value chain; entry barriers; sandboxes; GBA caveat |
| Closing | §§13–16 | Empty-seat unit cost; technology; synthesis; exam-style checklist |

## 1. What is the low-altitude economy?



```{=html}
<figure class="wdiag" id="w01-system" aria-labelledby="w01-system-title">
<p class="wdiag-cap" id="w01-system-title"><strong>LAE as a system (roles)</strong></p>
<div class="wdiag-flow">
<div class="wdiag-box"><strong>Customers / missions</strong><br/>Need time savings, access, inspection, logistics, or public service.</div>
<div class="wdiag-arrow" aria-hidden="true">↓</div>
<div class="wdiag-box"><strong>Operators</strong><br/>Deliver the flight or mission under applicable permissions.</div>
<div class="wdiag-arrow" aria-hidden="true">↓ spend on inputs</div>
<div class="wdiag-row">
<div class="wdiag-box"><strong>Aircraft</strong></div>
<div class="wdiag-box"><strong>Sites / pads</strong></div>
<div class="wdiag-box"><strong>Digital coordination</strong></div>
<div class="wdiag-box"><strong>Insurance &amp; services</strong></div>
</div>
</div>
<p class="wdiag-note">Roles only — not market shares or firm names. See also <a href="business-overview.qmd">How does LAE work?</a>.</p>
</figure>
```


[**Low-altitude economy (LAE)**](glossary.qmd#lae) means economic activity that uses low-altitude airspace — together with the aircraft, physical sites, digital systems, operators, customers, and supporting services needed to deliver a mission.

That definition is deliberately wide.

- If you only remember “flying cars,” you will miss most of the near-term economics: inspection, logistics, emergency response, and supporting services. OHKF projects those services as a large share of 2050 value added ([§5](#5-hong-kong-scale--and-how-to-read-the-hk350-billion-figure)).
- If you only remember “drones,” you will miss passenger concepts, infrastructure, and digital traffic management. You will also blur everyday speech with Cap. 448G’s legal label **SUA** (small unmanned aircraft).

### Policy band vs flying limits

In Hong Kong policy language, the working band is often described as airspace **generally below about 1,000 metres**. Issuers on this site include the 2024 Policy Address and LegCo paper CB(3)933/2024 ([Key figures](key-figures.qmd); [Readings](#readings)).

That **~1,000 m** figure is a **policy working description** of the *economic* field. It is **not** a Cap. 448G flying-height limit for small unmanned aircraft.

Cap. 448G sets operational height bands for ordinary categories:

- **100 ft AGL** (Category A1)
- **300 ft AGL ≈ 91 m** (Category A2)

unless CAD grants permission (G.N. 1276 of 2022; [Key figures](key-figures.qmd)). **AGL** means above ground level.

A student who conflates “LAE below 1,000 m” with “I may fly an SUA to 1,000 m” has mixed two layers of law and policy.

Keep the layers separate:

| Layer | What it is | What it is not |
|-------|------------|----------------|
| ~1,000 m working description | Policy / economic framing of LAE | A Cap. 448G flying ceiling |
| 100 ft / 300 ft AGL | Cap. 448G operating height bands (ordinary categories) | The same thing as the 1,000 m description |
| Mainland 120 m / 300 m (真高) labels | Mainland airspace scheme (国令761) | Hong Kong Cap. 448G |

Cite: [Key figures](key-figures.qmd) · [Glossary · altitude](glossary.qmd#altitude-scale) · [Official status](tracker.qmd).

Altitude language frames the *field*. The economic unit of analysis is still a **completed mission** — who needs an outcome, who flies, and who gets paid.

### One completed mission

Picture one completed mission, not one vehicle on a poster:

- Someone needs a delivery, inspection, medical transfer, or similar **outcome**.  
- An **operator** flies or manages the aircraft.  
- The craft needs somewhere to take off and land, energy, and maintenance.  
- Someone coordinates communications and traffic.  
- **Customers or mission sponsors** pay for the outcome.  
- Supporting services (finance, insurance, training, platforms) keep the operation going.

That whole chain is what this course means by LAE. Same idea in plain language: [What is LAE?](primer.qmd).

**Why start with the mission?** Commercial and policy questions attach to outcomes — time saved, risk avoided, access gained — not to airframe marketing. Week 1’s quantitative tools (VOT, generalized cost, unit cost) all measure *service* performance. Weeks 5–8 later ask whether sites and airspace can deliver that performance at scale.

Before the tools, keep **scope labels** distinct so “drone,” “SUA,” and “eVTOL” do not collapse into one legal claim.

### Scope labels (keep them distinct)

| Layer | What it covers |
|-------|----------------|
| **Aircraft in discussion** | Unmanned aircraft (everyday speech: “drones”), helicopters, and **eVTOL** concepts — **electric vertical take-off and landing** craft |
| **Physical infrastructure** | Take-off and landing sites (industry label: **vertiports**), charging, maintenance |
| **Digital infrastructure** | Communications, traffic-management software, data platforms |
| **Applications** | Logistics, inspection, emergency response, passenger transport, supporting finance and insurance |

Hong Kong law’s main label for light unmanned craft is **small unmanned aircraft (SUA)** under Cap. 448G (not more than **150 kg**). Weight classes run A1 → C (Category C, above 25 kg up to 150 kg, from **18 July 2025** — [Key figures](key-figures.qmd)). Everyday “drone” speech is **not** a Cap. 448G synonym.

**eVTOL** is an industry label. Hong Kong has **no dedicated eVTOL statute yet**. Heavier / passenger-oriented types sit above the SUA ceiling as **unconventional aircraft** pending rules ([Glossary · vehicles](glossary.qmd#vehicles-and-operations); [FAQ](faq.qmd)). When slides say “eVTOL,” treat it as a technology concept under discussion — not as a completed Hong Kong licensing category.

The exact altitude boundary also varies across jurisdictions. Mainland statistical / industrial-policy language for **低空经济** (low-altitude economy) is a separate frame. Do not treat it as the same metric as a Hong Kong value-added figure ([Glossary · Mainland](glossary.qmd#mainland-comparators)).

---

Section 1 defined LAE as a **mission system**. The next question is how that system differs, economically, from the scheduled aviation most people already know — because those differences drive cost, demand, and regulation for the rest of the course.

## 2. How LAE differs from traditional aviation

Traditional scheduled aviation typically uses large, expensive aircraft, large centralized airports, and long high-altitude flights. LAE points in a different business direction:

- **Short-distance, high-frequency** operations inside or between cities.  
- An **entire ecosystem** — sites, charging, digital coordination, insurance, maintenance — not only an airframe.  
- Different **cost structures**, operating models, and regulatory needs.

**Analogy used in class:** think less like a traditional airline network and more like a high-frequency network service for the sky — where waiting, access, and reliability matter as much as cruise speed.

**Managerial implication:** a fast aircraft does not automatically create a valuable *service*.

### What “different cost structure” means in practice

Three contrasts matter for later weeks:

1. [**Fixed cost**](glossary.qmd#fixed-cost) per passenger. A large jet spreads aircraft cost across hundreds of seats. Many eVTOL concepts under discussion have only a handful of seats (class examples often use four). Unit cost then rises sharply unless utilization and load factor are high ([§13](#13-the-empty-seat-problem-and-unit-cost)).  
2. **Ground and digital share of cost.** Vertiport fees, charging, and traffic-management services can claim a large slice of a short-trip fare ([§9](#9-the-lae-value-chain--who-creates-value-and-who-gets-paid)).  
3. **Operating-window sensitivity.** Noise or community limits that cut daily flights raise fixed cost per flight even if the aircraft is unchanged ([§9](#operating-restrictions-raise-unit-cost)).

None of these require inventing Hong Kong fare data. They are structural reasons LAE economics look different from long-haul airline economics.

---

Cost structure alone does not fix vocabulary. Policy papers, OEM decks, and Hong Kong readings mix **LAE**, **UAM**, and **AAM**. Before naming a use case, keep the nesting straight so you do not cite the wrong comparator as if it were Cap. 448G law.

## 3. LAE, UAM, and AAM

You will hear three acronyms constantly. Keep them **nested**, not interchangeable:

| Term | Meaning in this course |
|------|-------------------------|
| **LAE (low-altitude economy)** | The umbrella: economic activity in low-altitude airspace plus the supporting ecosystem. |
| [**UAM (urban air mobility)**](glossary.qmd#uam) | A *subset*: moving people or cargo over short distances **inside** a dense city. |
| [**AAM (advanced air mobility)**](glossary.qmd#aam) | A broader industry label for new aircraft connecting cities to suburbs or other corridors. |

**Course focus:** start **Hong Kong-first**, then expand to the **Greater Bay Area (GBA)** — the city cluster that includes Hong Kong, Macao, and nearby Guangdong cities — and selected Mainland / global comparators. EU / US / NASA-style AAM materials are **comparators**, not Hong Kong law ([Who decides what?](regulators.qmd); [Course overview](overview.qmd)).

### Why the nesting matters for analysis

- A **cargo SUA** trial under Cap. 448G may be LAE without being passenger UAM.  
- A **city-centre passenger** concept is UAM inside LAE.  
- An **inter-city corridor** concept is often discussed under AAM-style language — still not automatic Hong Kong law, and not the same as claiming a GBA corridor is already day-to-day service ([§12](#12-working-with-the-greater-bay-area)).  

When a reading uses “UAM” or “AAM,” ask which part of the LAE umbrella it actually covers — and which Hong Kong legal pathway (SUA vs unconventional aircraft vs planned rules) would apply.

---

With the umbrella terms sorted, ask what **customer problem** a service actually solves. Week 1 groups near-term opportunities into four families; later weeks test whether any one family clears cost, capacity, and acceptance screens.

## 4. Four ways to create value in the sky

An LAE service must solve a customer problem better than existing alternatives. Week 1 organises opportunities into four families:

1. **Cargo and logistics** — high-priority items where speed, reliability, or access matters.  
2. **Passenger air mobility** — premium short-distance travel where door-to-door time savings can justify the fare.  
3. **Industrial inspection** — bridges, buildings, power assets, and remote sites with less disruption and risk.  
4. **Emergency and public services** — medical delivery, emergency response, search and rescue, environmental monitoring.

**Managerial question:** which applications create enough value to cover cost, risk, and regulatory requirements?

### How to read each family economically

| Family | Typical value created | Typical binding constraints (preview) |
|--------|----------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Cargo / logistics | Time, reliability, access where roads are slow or blocked | Payload, weather, landing sites, BVLOS / advanced-ops permission ([**BVLOS**](glossary.qmd#bvlos) = beyond visual line of sight) |
| Passenger mobility | Door-to-door time vs MTR / taxi / Airport Express | Vertiport access, load factor, noise, public acceptance |
| Inspection | Lower disruption and risk vs manned access | Safety case, data / privacy, repeatability |
| Emergency / public | Outcomes that alternatives cannot match in time | Priority rules, funding (availability vs usage), acceptance |

Dated trial and operating examples on this site: [Use cases](usecases.qmd). Named organisations: [Companies & sectors](landscape.qmd). Do **not** invent firm counts or route performance here — cite those pages when you need issuer-backed examples.

Icebreaker intuition from class (not a claim that either service is operating today): an urgent medical delivery that avoids harbour road congestion, or a business-district–airport air link that cuts door-to-door time, both illustrate *why* LAE is discussed. Whether either is commercially or socially viable is exactly what Weeks 1–10 teach you to test.

---

Value families are global; this course is **Hong Kong-first**. Scale claims therefore need careful attribution — especially the widely quoted HK$350 billion projection.

## 5. Hong Kong scale — and how to read the HK$350 billion figure

Why might LAE matter for Hong Kong? Low-altitude airspace adds a **third dimension** to the transport and logistics network. Policy already treats LAE as a development theme: the **2024 Policy Address** describes economic activities generally below 1,000 metres and establishes the Working Group on Developing Low-altitude Economy ([Readings](#readings); [Timeline](dates.qmd)).

### The HK$350 billion projection



```{=html}
<figure class="wdiag" id="w01-ohkf" aria-labelledby="w01-ohkf-title">
<p class="wdiag-cap" id="w01-ohkf-title"><strong>Reading the OHKF HK$350bn figure</strong></p>
<div class="wdiag-stack cols-2">
<div class="wdiag-box fact"><strong>What it is</strong><br/>Our Hong Kong Foundation (private think-tank) scenario projection for Hong Kong industry <em>value added</em> by 2050; supporting services are the majority in that report.</div>
<div class="wdiag-box muted"><strong>What it is not</strong><br/>Not a government target; not operator revenue; not automatic GDP; not a single firm’s obtainable market.</div>
</div>
<p class="wdiag-note">Cite Key figures / Readings. Do not merge with Mainland scale totals.</p>
</figure>
```


You will also see a private projection: that Hong Kong’s LAE-related industries could generate about **HK$350 billion** in annual **industry value added by 2050**, with a large share in supporting services.

That figure comes from **Our Hong Kong Foundation (OHKF)** (*Taking Flight: Forging a Future for Hong Kong’s Low-Altitude Economy*, September 2025). It is a **think-tank projection**, **not** an HKSAR government number.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Attribution rule.** When you quote **HK$350bn**, name **OHKF**, the metric (**industry value added**), the geography (**Hong Kong**), and the horizon (**2050**). Do not call it a government target, GDP, operator revenue, or a Mainland 规模 total. Cite: [Key figures](key-figures.qmd) · [Common questions](faq.qmd) · [Official status](tracker.qmd) · [Readings](#readings).
:::

**Why the metric matters.** **Value added** subtracts intermediate inputs. It is not the same as summing ticket revenue across operators. Week 9 returns to this distinction when market-sizing meets social impact ([Week 9](week-09.qmd)).

### Services-layer hypothesis

Hong Kong’s possible comparative advantage is often framed as a **service layer** — finance and leasing, insurance and risk management, legal / certification / professional services, digital platforms, and international business development — sitting alongside GBA strengths in manufacturing, electronics, batteries, and large-scale testing.

That is a **strategic proposition to evaluate**, not a predetermined outcome. OHKF’s emphasis on supporting services in the 2050 projection is consistent with that framing — but consistency with a think-tank narrative is not proof of comparative advantage. You still need capability, cost, regulation, demand, and competition evidence (Week 12 returns to leasing and service roles).

## 6. Value of time and net present value

Sections 1–5 defined the field. Sections 6–8 open the **quantitative toolkit**. The goal is not memorising symbols — it is knowing which question each tool answers.

### Value of time (VOT)

**Value of time (VOT)** expresses how much a customer is willing to pay to save travel (or delivery) time. It is not a universal constant: it varies across customers, trip purposes, and situations. Saving twenty minutes may be worth far more for an urgent medical delivery than for a routine errand.

Time-related benefit per trip:



$$
\text{Value of time saved per trip} = \text{VOT} \times \Delta T
$$



where $\Delta T$ is time saved relative to the best alternative (same time units as VOT).

**Intuition.** VOT converts minutes into money so you can compare a faster but dearer option with a slower but cheaper one. It does **not** by itself tell you demand volume, load factor, or NPV.

Customer value is only step one. Investors still ask whether the **cash stream**, after costs and risk, justifies what must be spent today — that is NPV.

### Net present value (NPV)

**Net present value (NPV)** asks whether the future cash a project generates is enough to justify the investment made today, under stated assumptions:



$$
\text{NPV} = -\text{Initial investment} + \text{Present value of future profits}
$$



| NPV result (under stated assumptions) | Interpretation |
|---------------------------------------|----------------|
| Positive | Project may be financially attractive |
| Negative | Does not justify the investment |

NPV is not a guarantee — it is a disciplined way to organise cash, timing, and risk later in the course. Week 6’s staging / real-options logic and Week 9’s downside analysis refine what “under stated assumptions” means.

Put VOT and NPV on one screen with a middle step — **capture** — so time savings are not mistaken for automatic profit.

### A three-step viability screen

1. **Does the service create value for customers?** (for example via time savings: $\text{VOT}\times\Delta T$).  
2. **Can the operator capture enough of that value?**  
   

$$
   \text{Annual operating profit} = \text{Annual revenue} - \text{Annual operating cost}
   $$

  
3. **Does the project justify the initial investment?** (NPV).

**Core lesson:** time savings support willingness to pay, but fare, demand, costs, and investment determine financial viability.

### Connecting the three steps (worked intuition)

Suppose door-to-door time savings are worth HK$500 per trip under a high VOT ([§8.1](#81-door-to-door-friction-destroys-value)). That is step 1 — **customer value**.

Step 2 asks whether the operator can **charge** something related to that value *and* cover operating cost after paying partners (vertiport, energy, insurance — [§9](#illustrative-unit-economics-not-market-data)). If the fare is only HK$200 after partners take HK$200 of a HK$300 ticket, the operator’s margin can vanish under a small fare cut.

Step 3 asks whether the **stream** of margins, after tax and risk, covers the upfront aircraft, site, and compliance investment (NPV). A sandbox may change step 3 by reducing delay and uncertainty ([§11](#11-regulatory-sandboxes-in-hong-kong)) — it does not invent positive margins.

---

VOT and NPV tell you what time is worth and whether investment might pay. Travellers still choose among **modes**. Generalized cost puts money and time on one scale so you can see when a faster air option can (and cannot) beat MTR, taxi, or Airport Express.

## 7. Generalized cost and mode choice

When travellers choose among MTR, taxi, or a hypothetical air taxi, they consider more than the ticket price:

- **Money cost** — fare and related charges.  
- **Time cost** — in-vehicle time, waiting, boarding, and transfers.  
- **Other factors** — reliability, convenience, comfort, perceived safety.

Economists often combine money and time into [**generalized cost (GC)**](glossary.qmd#generalised-cost):



$$
\text{Generalized cost} = \text{Ticket price} + \text{VOT} \times \text{Travel time}
$$



All else equal, the customer prefers the option with **lower** generalized cost. A faster mode can charge more, but **only up to the value of the time it actually saves** on the full journey.

**Design implication:** plan the **complete journey**, not only cruise time in the air. Week 4 returns to demand and mode choice ([Week 4](week-04.qmd)).

### How GC connects to VOT and to fare caps

Rearrange the indifference condition. If the alternative mode has generalized cost $GC_A$ and the air option takes time $T_{\text{air}}$, the maximum fare that keeps the traveller indifferent (ignoring comfort and reliability) is:



$$
P_{\max} = GC_A - \text{VOT}\times T_{\text{air}}
$$



That is exactly the Airport Express screen in [§8.2](#82-finding-a-maximum-ticket-price-against-airport-express). Notice what is missing: waiting at the vertiport, access time to the pad, cancellation risk, and perceived safety. Adding friction raises $T_{\text{air}}$ or lowers effective VOT for the air option — which is why [§8.1](#81-door-to-door-friction-destroys-value) destroys value even when cruise time is unchanged.

---

The formulas are short; mistakes usually come from **wrong door-to-door times** or from treating a classroom fare ceiling as a forecast. The next examples apply VOT and GC under stated assumptions — then connect the answers to partner payments and unit cost.

## 8. Worked illustrations (classroom assumptions)

The next two examples apply VOT and generalized cost. Figures are **illustrative** — see the callout under [Summary](#summary). They are **not** claims about current Airport Express demand or any operating air-taxi fare.

### 8.1 Door-to-door friction destroys value

**Scenario (illustrative):** a proposed air-taxi link between Hong Kong International Airport and Central. Traveller’s time worth **HK$1,000 per hour**.

| | Case A: smooth journey | Case B: friction shock |
|--|------------------------|-------------------------|
| Flight time | 10 minutes | 10 minutes |
| Boarding and waiting | 5 minutes | 25 minutes |
| Total journey | 15 minutes | 35 minutes |
| Time saved vs a 45-minute alternative | 30 minutes = 0.5 h | 10 minutes ≈ 0.167 h |
| Value of time saved | $1000\times 0.5 =$ **HK$500** | $1000\times 0.167 \approx$ **HK$167** |

**Takeaway:** a fast aircraft does not guarantee a valuable service. Waiting, transfers, and access time can sharply reduce the fare premium customers will accept.

**Connecting idea.** Case B is not “bad luck.” It is what happens when vertiport processing, security, or schedule padding is ignored in the business case. Infrastructure economics (Week 5) and public acceptance / operating windows (Weeks 9–10) re-enter here as determinants of $\Delta T$, not as separate soft topics.

### 8.2 Finding a maximum ticket price against Airport Express

**Scenario (illustrative):** what is the most a time-sensitive traveller would pay for an air taxi before choosing the Airport Express? Assume **VOT = HK$10 per minute**.

**Airport Express (assumed for the exercise):** ticket HK$115; journey 24 minutes. (The HK$115 figure is used as a classroom anchor for the formula — treat it as part of the illustrative setup, not as a claim about every fare class or access journey.)



$$
GC_{\text{MTR}} = 115 + 10\times 24 = \mathbf{HK\$355}
$$



**Air taxi (assumed):** journey 8 minutes. Match the same generalized cost:



$$
P + 10\times 8 = 355 \implies P = \mathbf{HK\$275}
$$



Under these simplified assumptions, **HK$275** makes the traveller indifferent. Actual demand also depends on waiting, access, reliability, comfort, and perceived safety — none of which are in the short formula.

**Connecting idea.** $P=\text{HK\$275}$ is a **ceiling under stated assumptions**, not a forecast price. If partner payments alone claim HK$200 of a HK$300 ticket ([§9](#illustrative-unit-economics-not-market-data)), a fare near HK$275 may still leave a thin operator margin — connecting GC to value-chain capture.

### 8.3 How the Week 1 tools fit on one page

| Tool | Answers | Feeds into |
|------|---------|------------|
| VOT × ΔT | How much time savings are *worth* | Willingness to pay; GC |
| Generalized cost | Which mode wins on money + time | Maximum fare; demand sketches (Week 4) |
| Ticket split | Who captures the fare | Operator margin; partner bargaining |
| Cost per passenger | Fixed cost ÷ (flights × seats × load) | Fare floor before profit |
| NPV | Whether investment is justified | Staging / sandbox learning (Week 6–7) |

A coherent Week 1 answer moves **down** this table: customer value → mode comparison → capture → unit cost → investment — without double-counting the same constraint twice.

---

Tools answered what customers might pay. The value chain asks **who receives** that payment — OEMs, sites, digital services, insurers, and the operator — and why a thin operator margin can coexist with a high ticket.

## 9. The LAE value chain — who creates value and who gets paid?

Concepts and tools are in place. This section asks **who makes what** along the chain.

### Roles

| Role | Plain meaning |
|------|----------------|
| [**OEM**](glossary.qmd#oem) | **Original equipment manufacturer** — produces the aircraft or key components. |
| **Vertiport / sites** | Take-off, landing, passenger or cargo handling, charging, related ground operations (industry language; no dedicated Hong Kong vertiport statute yet). |
| **UTM / U-space** | Digital services and procedures that support safe, efficient management of unmanned operations. **UTM** = unmanned aircraft system traffic management. **U-space** is an EU / industry frame, **not** Hong Kong law; Hong Kong’s Smart Low-altitude Traffic Management System is a **planned** programme (Policy Address language: progressive implementation from **2028**), not a statute yet ([Key figures](key-figures.qmd); [Glossary · airspace](glossary.qmd#airspace-and-traffic)). |
| **Operator** | Provides the transport, logistics, inspection, or public service to the customer. |
| **Customers / public agencies** | Pay for missions or sponsor public-service outcomes. |
| **Supporting services** | Finance, leasing, insurance, certification, legal and professional services. |

Roles-only money-and-value map (no firm names): [How does LAE work?](business-overview.qmd). Named organisations: [Companies & sectors](landscape.qmd).

**Verified planning fact to keep attached to UTM:** progressive implementation of Hong Kong’s Smart Low-altitude Traffic Management System is described as **from 2028** in Policy Address language tracked on [Key figures](key-figures.qmd) (WATCH). That is a **target / planning statement**, not a claim that city-wide UTM already exists — and it is **not** the same as saying Hong Kong “has U-space.”

### How a ticket price might be shared

One teaching decomposition of an air-taxi fare:



$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Ticket price} =\ &\text{Aircraft cost} + \text{Vertiport fee} + \text{Energy} \\
&+ \text{UTM fee} + \text{Maintenance and labour} \\
&+ \text{Insurance and overhead} + \text{Operator margin}.
\end{aligned}
$$



Different participants may charge usage fees, lease payments, or service fees. The **operator** typically faces direct demand risk (attract customers; fill capacity). Infrastructure and platform providers may face less *direct* passenger risk, but they still depend on traffic volume and bear investment, technology, and regulatory risk.

**Core lesson:** creating value does not guarantee capturing value. Contract design and bargaining power determine how revenue is shared.

### Illustrative unit economics (not market data)

Suppose a passenger pays **HK$300**. One classroom allocation:

| Payment | Amount |
|---------|--------|
| Vertiport fee | HK$100 |
| UTM and digital services | HK$20 |
| Insurance and financing | HK$30 |
| Aircraft lease allocation | HK$50 |
| **Partner payments** | **HK$200** |
| Cash left for operator | HK$100 |
| Energy | HK$20 |
| Maintenance and labour | HK$50 |
| **Operator margin** | **HK$30** |

If all costs stayed unchanged, cutting the fare by HK$50 would turn a HK$30 margin into a HK$20 loss. Real contracts differ; the point is **sensitivity**, not the specific split.

**Connecting idea.** Compare this margin with the GC ceiling of HK$275 in §8.2. Under those two *separate* classroom setups, the operator is already near a knife-edge: customer indifference is not the same as a thick margin after partners are paid. Week 3’s revenue management and Week 6’s partnership payment design exist because this tension is structural.

### Stakeholder conflict and externalities

An [**externality**](glossary.qmd#externality) arises when an activity imposes costs or benefits on others that are not fully reflected in the decision-maker’s private costs or revenues.

- **Operators** want enough flights and passengers to cover fixed costs.  
- **Investors** want a credible path to approval, revenue, and scale.  
- **Government** balances innovation, safety, efficiency, and public interest.  
- **Communities** care about noise, privacy, visual impact, and fair access to benefits.

**Managerial challenge:** how can a service reach commercial scale while maintaining public acceptance?

Acceptance is not only reputation. When communities or rules shrink the operating window, **fixed cost per flight** rises — the next classroom screen.

### Operating restrictions raise unit cost

**Scenario (illustrative):** noise concerns restrict evening and overnight flights. Fixed aircraft lease cost = **HK$10,000 per day**.

| | Wider window | Restricted window |
|--|--------------|-------------------|
| Flights per day | 50 | 20 |
| Fixed cost per flight | HK$10,000 / 50 = **HK$200** | HK$10,000 / 20 = **HK$500** |

Public acceptance is not only a communications issue. Operating limits change utilization, unit costs, and commercial viability. Weeks 8–10 return to congestion, noise, privacy, and social impact.

**Connection.** The same HK$10,000/day fixed cost reappears in the empty-seat unit-cost equation ([§13](#13-the-empty-seat-problem-and-unit-cost)). Restrictions that cut flights are economically equivalent to a utilization shock.

---

Even a clean ticket split fails if the product cannot enter. Aviation’s safety culture and certification timelines raise [**entry barriers**](glossary.qmd#entry-barrier); that is the economic reason controlled trial programmes exist — not a waiver of Cap. 448G or airworthiness duties.

## 10. Why new aviation products face high entry barriers

Aviation is extremely safety-regulated. Certifying a new type for routine public use can take many years and very large compliance outlays under traditional manned-aviation pathways (class discussion often refers to stringent airworthiness regimes such as US “Part 25”-style certification as a *comparator*, not as Hong Kong SUA law).

For startups and new mission designs, a multi-year wait before the first paying customer can exhaust capital. That tension motivates **controlled trial** programmes: test selected applications under approved routes and conditions, collect evidence, and reduce uncertainty *before* committing to full-scale deployment — without pretending that safety rules disappear.

**Hong Kong pathway reminder.** Light unmanned operations sit under Cap. **448G** with a risk-based approach (full effect **1 December 2022**; Category C expansion **July 2025** — [Week 7 Readings](week-07.qmd) / [Key figures](key-figures.qmd)). That is a different legal track from traditional large-aircraft certification — but advanced operations still need prior CAD permission, and sandboxes still do not waive safety.

---

Hong Kong’s answer to “learn before you scale” is the **regulatory sandbox** track — actually more than one programme. Keep the labels separate before you treat trial evidence as a commercial franchise.

## 11. Regulatory sandboxes in Hong Kong

A **regulatory sandbox** allows companies and public agencies to test selected LAE applications under controlled conditions. In economic terms it aims to:

- **Test safely** on approved routes and operating conditions.  
- **Learn early** — evidence for firms and regulators before wider deployment.  
- **Reduce uncertainty** — surface problems before very large irreversible investments.  
- **Inform regulation** — trial results help shape operating and safety requirements.

**A sandbox does not remove safety requirements.** It is a controlled pathway for testing and learning.

### Keep two Hong Kong programmes separate

Hong Kong has run more than one trial track. On this site you must **not** merge them:

| Programme | How to treat it (issuer-backed counts) |
|-----------|----------------------------------------|
| Early **Regulatory Sandbox** | First-batch selection **38 of 72** projects (GIA, 20 Mar 2025). Later Policy Address language may refer to larger counts of regularised projects — those are **different** snapshots, not a substitute for the first-batch figure. |
| Later **Sandbox X** | Distinct programme. Selected modules reported as **33** so far on TLB materials: UTM **15** + unconventional aircraft **4** + shared platform **5** + others **9**. A Policy Address snapshot of “~10” projects that had begun testing is **not** the same as the 33 module total ([Key figures](key-figures.qmd)). |

Citeable counts and issuers: [Key figures](key-figures.qmd) · [Official status](tracker.qmd) · [Who decides what? · standing caveats](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats) · [FAQ](faq.qmd). Later weeks carry AC-013 (BVLOS in the first Regulatory Sandbox) and AC-017 (Sandbox X cross-boundary) — do not mix those circulars ([Week 7](week-07.qmd); [Week 8](week-08.qmd)).

With programmes named correctly, summarise economically what a sandbox can change in the **entry-barrier** sum.

### Entry barriers as a simple sum



$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Entry barrier} =\ &\text{Investment cost} + \text{Compliance cost} \\
&+ \text{Cost of delay} + \text{Uncertainty}.
\end{aligned}
$$



| Component | Plain meaning |
|-----------|----------------|
| **Investment cost** | Aircraft, infrastructure, software, staff |
| **Compliance cost** | Testing, documentation, professional services, approvals |
| **Cost of delay** | Cash spent while waiting before wider operation |
| **Uncertainty** | Technology, business model, or approval pathway may not work as expected |

**Core lesson:** a sandbox may reduce **delay** and **uncertainty**, making a project easier to test and finance. It does **not** eliminate compliance or safety costs.

Without early controlled trials, firms often face larger upfront commitments, slower operational learning, and greater risk of expensive redesign. With a sandbox, tests can be staged, evidence arrives earlier, and investment can be linked to milestones. The main economic value is **faster, lower-cost learning under controlled conditions**.

**Link to NPV.** Lower delay and uncertainty improve the *distribution* of possible NPVs (Week 9). They do not magically create positive contribution after partner payments ([§9](#illustrative-unit-economics-not-market-data)).

---

Sandbox learning is local; supply chains and corridor ideas are regional. Hong Kong’s LAE story is often told together with the **Greater Bay Area** — manufacturing and testing nearby, services in Hong Kong — but corridor language must stay evidence-disciplined.

## 12. Working with the Greater Bay Area

Hong Kong’s LAE development is closely connected with the wider GBA ecosystem:

- **Manufacturing and technology** strengths in Shenzhen and other GBA cities (drones, electronics, batteries, supply chains).  
- **Hong Kong capabilities** in international finance, insurance, legal and professional services, logistics, and a dense urban testing environment.  
- **Cross-boundary logistics and public-service ideas** that would need coordination on routes, customs, data, communications, and safety.

**Strategic question:** how can Hong Kong and other GBA cities combine complementary strengths rather than duplicate them?

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**Evidence caveat.** A Shenzhen–Hong Kong / GBA cross-boundary corridor appears in policy discussion, but on the evidence tracked on this site it is **not** flying as day-to-day operating corridor service. Treat corridor language as **planned / under discussion**, not as current operations ([Regulators · standing caveats](regulators.qmd#standing-caveats); [Official status](tracker.qmd); [What is LAE?](primer.qmd)). Sandbox X may include cross-boundary *trials* under AC-017 — trials are not the same as a scheduled corridor product.
:::

---

GBA strategy does not fix aircraft economics. Many passenger concepts under discussion have few seats: unless **utilization and load factor** are high, fixed cost per passenger stays above what generalized-cost fare ceilings can support.

## 13. The empty-seat problem and unit cost

Airlines amortise expensive aircraft across hundreds of seats. Many eVTOL concepts under discussion have only a handful of seats (class examples often use **four**). You cannot divide pilot and machine cost by 300; you divide by a small number. Unless utilization and load factor are high, ticket prices rise sharply.

[**Utilization**](glossary.qmd#utilization) = how often the aircraft flies. [**Load factor**](glossary.qmd#load-factor) = share of seats that are filled.

[Unit cost](glossary.qmd#unit-cost):



$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Cost per passenger}
=\ &\text{Variable cost per passenger} \\
&+ \frac{\text{Daily fixed cost}}{\text{Flights per day}\times\text{Seats per flight}\times\text{Load factor}}.
\end{aligned}
$$



| Driver | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **Utilization** | How frequently the aircraft flies |
| **Capacity** | Seats available |
| **Load factor** | Share of seats actually occupied |

**Core lesson:** operators need both frequent operations *and* sufficient demand. Flying often does not help if the aircraft repeatedly flies empty.

### Illustrative comparison

**Assumptions (classroom):** fixed aircraft cost = HK$10,000/day; variable cost = HK$100/flight; four seats.

| | Case A: 10 flights, 50% load | Case B: 25 flights, 80% load |
|--|------------------------------|------------------------------|
| Paying passengers | $10\times 4\times 0.5 = 20$ | $25\times 4\times 0.8 = 80$ |
| Fixed cost per passenger | HK$500 | HK$125 |
| Variable cost per passenger | HK$50 | HK$31.25 |
| **Total cost per passenger** | **HK$550** | **HK$156.25** |

Technology may help, but demand, load factor, charging, maintenance, infrastructure, weather, and regulation all affect achievable utilization. Week 3 develops cost structures and revenue management ([Week 3](week-03.qmd)).

**Connecting idea.** Case A’s HK$550 cost per passenger sits far above the illustrative GC fare ceiling of HK$275 in §8.2. Under those two classroom setups, the service cannot clear both a customer indifference fare and a low-utilization cost floor. That is the empty-seat problem in one sentence: **customer value and aircraft economics must meet in the middle.**

---

Unit cost and fare ceilings set the economic target. **Technology** matters when it moves those levers — shorter door-to-door time, higher reliable flights per day, lower energy or maintenance — not when it only improves a brochure.

## 14. Technology as an economic tool

Treat technology as a lever on economics, not as an end in itself:

- **Aircraft technology** changes speed, range, payload, capacity, reliability, and operating cost.  
- **Automation** may reduce crew needs and support frequency — but must still satisfy safety and regulatory requirements.  
- **UTM and communications** support coordination and scale in complex airspace.  
- **Infrastructure** — charging, maintenance, landing sites, passenger processing — determines actual throughput.

**Managerial lesson:** a technically impressive aircraft creates commercial value only when the **complete operating system** is safe, reliable, convenient, and affordable.

**Tie-back.** Technology that cuts boarding time raises $\Delta T$ and VOT-based willingness to pay ([§8.1](#81-door-to-door-friction-destroys-value)). Technology that raises daily flights lowers fixed cost per passenger ([§13](#13-the-empty-seat-problem-and-unit-cost)). Technology that only looks good on a poster does neither.

---

Pull the thread: system definition → value → Hong Kong scale with correct attribution → VOT / GC / NPV → who gets paid → sandboxes kept distinct → GBA caveat → empty-seat unit cost → technology as a lever.

## 15. Putting Week 1 together

LAE is a **system**: aircraft, infrastructure, digital coordination, operators, customers, and supporting services. A service creates value when it saves time, cuts cost or risk, improves access, or enables a mission alternatives cannot do well. Commercial viability still hangs on willingness to pay, demand, utilization, load factor, operating cost, and investment cost.

Hong Kong may hold advantages in selected high-value services and in connecting GBA capabilities — as a hypothesis to test with evidence. Regulatory sandboxes support controlled testing and faster learning; they do not waive safety or compliance. Technology matters when it improves the economics of the **full service**, not only the airframe.

Keep **Sandbox ≠ Sandbox X**. Attribute **HK$350bn** only to OHKF (value added, Hong Kong, 2050). Do not claim cross-boundary corridors as day-to-day service. Keep ~1,000 m policy language separate from Cap. 448G flying limits.

The short checklist is in [Summary](#summary) above.

---

## 16. Study checklist

Use this when reviewing — each item should be answerable in your own words with a formula or a cite:

1. Define LAE as a **mission system**, not an airframe.  
2. State the difference between **~1,000 m** policy language and **100 ft / 300 ft** Cap. 448G bands.  
3. Nest **LAE ⊃ UAM** and place **AAM** as a broader industry label; name the course’s Hong Kong-first focus.  
4. Compute $\text{VOT}\times\Delta T$ and explain why friction destroys value.  
5. Compute generalized cost and a maximum fare against an alternative.  
6. Split a ticket and show how a fare cut can erase operator margin.  
7. Show how an operating-window cut raises fixed cost per flight.  
8. Write the entry-barrier sum and say what a sandbox can and cannot reduce.  
9. Keep **38 of 72** (first Sandbox batch) separate from Sandbox X **33** modules / “~10 begun testing.”  
10. Apply the empty-seat unit-cost equation and interpret utilization × load factor.  
11. Quote OHKF **HK$350bn** with correct metric, geography, horizon, and non-government attribution.  
12. State the GBA corridor caveat: policy discussion ≠ day-to-day operating service.
